title: Germany's shortage occupations: is your profession on the list?
description: Germany keeps an official list of occupations with a shortage of workers. What it means for your visa, how to check your profession and what to do next.
html:
Germany's economy is short of workers in a long list of professions, from nursing to software development, and the immigration rules reward people who fill those gaps. If your occupation is on the official shortage list, several visa routes become easier. This guide explains what the list is and how to use it.

What a shortage occupation is

The Federal Employment Agency analyses job vacancies, unemployment and the time it takes to fill positions, and publishes a list of occupations where demand clearly exceeds supply. The list is updated regularly and currently contains well over a hundred occupations across healthcare, engineering, IT, skilled trades, education and transport.

Why Germany needs workers from abroad

An ageing population and a shrinking domestic workforce mean that the country needs several hundred thousand additional workers every year just to keep its economy at its current size. Immigration law has been rewritten twice in the last decade to make it easier for qualified people to come.

Which jobs are in demand

Nurses, doctors and care workers head the list. Engineers in mechanical, electrical, civil and automation fields follow, along with software developers, IT administrators and data specialists. Skilled trades such as electricians, plumbers, HVAC technicians and construction specialists are chronically short. Teachers, train drivers, truck drivers and childcare workers round out the picture.

How to check

The Federal Employment Agency publishes the list on its website; the make-it-in-germany portal offers a searchable version in English. Search for your occupation, not your degree title; the list is organised by job.

What it means for your visa

Being in a shortage occupation earns a point under the Opportunity Card scheme, lowers the salary threshold for an EU Blue Card in some fields and, for skilled trades, opens the recognition partnership route, under which you can start working while your qualification is still being recognised. Employers in these fields are also more willing to support relocation.

Getting started

Have your qualification recognised, or at least start the process, since that is the gate for every route. Check the language requirement for your field; nursing and teaching require German, IT often does not. Then apply for the route that fits: a job offer plus a work visa or Blue Card, or the Opportunity Card to search from inside Germany. Whichever route you take, the financial proof and health insurance requirements are the same, and they can be arranged before you travel.
